extracted.intended_audience: students and readers of English poetry; literary critics
extracted.subtask_description: Criteria and critical principles for judging English poetry (style, versification, satire, lyric and descriptive power) as discussed in a lecture-format literary criticism. Focuses on qualities to look for and common faults to avoid.

rubrics_metrics.name: Conciseness and felicity of expression
rubrics_metrics.description: The conciseness and felicity of the expression are equally remarkable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Praised as a mark of genius in shorter utterances and aphoristic criticism; implies clear, compact wording that conveys thought effectively.

rubrics_metrics.name: Originality of remarks and illustrations
rubrics_metrics.description: Nothing can be more original and happy than the general remarks and illustrations in the Essay.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Original, felicitous illustrations and observations are highly valued; avoid merely repeating received commonplaces.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoidance of narrow, school-bound critical rules
rubrics_metrics.description: The critical rules laid down are too much those of a school, and of a confined one.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Critical principles should not be rigidly sectarian or confined to a single school's watchwords; beware formulas that stifle judgement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Eloquent enthusiasm for literary greatness
rubrics_metrics.description: The author speaks with eloquent enthusiasm of the fame of ancient writers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ability to celebrate high literary achievement with genuine, elevated feeling enhances a critic's or poet's authority and persuasive power.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rhyme and sound must echo the sense
rubrics_metrics.description: 'Tis not enough no harshness gives offence; The sound must seem an echo to the sense.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rhyme and sonic qualities should arise naturally from meaning; avoid forcing rhyme at the expense of sense or natural sound.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid repetitive cant or overused watchwords
rubrics_metrics.description: There is a cant in the present day about genius ... it was a kind of watchword ... In Essay on Criticism there are no less than half a score successive couplets rhyming to the word sense.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Excessive repetition of a single word or slogan (a cant) weakens poetry and criticism; vary diction and avoid catchphrases that become meaningless through repetition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Grammatical and logical correctness
rubrics_metrics.description: His grammatical construction is often lame and imperfect. Example: 'There died the best of passions, Love and Fame.' This is not a legitimate ellipsis; Fame is not a passion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Maintain grammatical propriety and logical coherence; avoid illegitimate ellipses or constructions that confuse sense for the sake of sound.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rhymes should be to the ear, not merely to the eye
rubrics_metrics.description: Pope's rhymes are constantly defective, being rhymes to the eye instead of the ear.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prioritize auditory effect over printed spelling; a good rhyme convinces when read aloud, not just when looked at on the page.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid changing grammatical tense for rhyme
rubrics_metrics.description: In the translation of the Iliad ... he continually changes the tenses in the same sentence for the purposes of the rhyme.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not sacrifice grammatical consistency or logical sequence to achieve rhyme; such shifts indicate technical weakness or inattention to exactness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Emotional authenticity in love-poetry
rubrics_metrics.description: The Epistle of Eloise to Abelard is fine as a poem and finer as a piece of high-wrought eloquence ... The tears shed are drops gushing from the heart: the words are burning sighs breathed from the soul of love.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Love-poetry should convey genuine feeling and intimacy — words that seem to come from heartfelt experience rather than contrivance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid verbosity that outspins the argument
rubrics_metrics.description: He spins the thread of his verbosity finer than the staple of his argument.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Poetry or didactic verse must not allow ornate language or prolixity to overwhelm or replace substantive argument or thought.

rubrics_metrics.name: Satirical force and moral invective
rubrics_metrics.description: The finest burst of severe moral invective ... 'Virtue may chuse the high or low degree ...' The Dunciad has splendid passages ...
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Effective satire combines moral energy and clear invective; it should expose vice with force and dignity rather than petty spite.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid petulant or effeminate enmity in satire
rubrics_metrics.description: His enmity is effeminate and petulant from a sense of weakness ... his Satires are not in general so good as his Epistles.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Satire loses power if it feels petty, peevish, or rooted in weakness rather than righteous indignation; restraint and moral seriousness improve satirical impact.

rubrics_metrics.name: Best personal satire blends respect with cutting sense of failings
rubrics_metrics.description: The finest piece of personal satire in Pope is of a mixed kind, made up of his respect for the man, and a cutting sense of his failings.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A powerful personal satire balances admiration or understanding of the subject with incisive criticism — cruelty or pure malice should be avoided.

rubrics_metrics.name: Compliments crafted with high value
rubrics_metrics.description: His compliments are divine; they are equal in value to a house or an estate.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Skillful, elevated compliments (or praise) are an art in themselves and can confer high rhetorical worth; phrase-making here is valuable and consequential.

rubrics_metrics.name: Humour vs. wit (definition and balance)
rubrics_metrics.description: Humour is the making others act or talk absurdly and unconsciously: wit is the pointing out and ridiculing that absurdity consciously, and with more or less ill-nature.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Distinguish and balance humour (observational, arising from character/action) with wit (deliberate, often sharper ridicule); excessive wit without humour can feel ill-natured.

rubrics_metrics.name: Balance wit with story and other elements
rubrics_metrics.description: The fault of Butler's poem is not that it has too much wit, but that it has not an equal quantity of other things (no story, little humour).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Wit must be integrated with narrative, character, or humour to create a satisfying whole; wit alone can produce an arid work.

rubrics_metrics.name: Satirical portraiture: fidelity vs. refinement
rubrics_metrics.description: Dryden seems to grapple with his antagonists, and to describe real persons; Pope seems to refine upon them in his own mind, making them what he pleases, until they are not real characters.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Decide whether satire should aim at faithful, observed portraiture or at stylized refinement; the former grounds satire in reality, the latter risks caricature and repetitive spleen.

rubrics_metrics.name: Variety and vigour of versification
rubrics_metrics.description: Dryden's versification contains the finest examples of varied and sounding versification; Pope's praise of versification must be confined to its uniform smoothness and harmony.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Variety and sonorousness in metre and line are virtues; uniform smoothness can be admired but may lack force or variety.

rubrics_metrics.name: Lyrical poetry depends on selection of images
rubrics_metrics.description: Lyrical poetry ... deals in hieroglyphics and passing figures, which depend for effect, not on the working out, but on the selection. It is the dance and pantomime of poetry.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Lyric success rests on choosing striking, emblematic images rather than elaborate development; selection and musicality matter more than epic breadth.

rubrics_metrics.name: Descriptive poetry should convey the whole impression
rubrics_metrics.description: Thomson ... gives most of the poetry of natural description. He describes the vivid impression which the whole makes upon his own imagination ... not to the eye alone, but to the other senses, and to the whole man.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Good descriptive verse transfers an unbroken, multi-sensory impression — atmosphere, sound, temperature, motion — rather than cataloguing minute particulars alone.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid reliance on trite commonplaces and mechanical imagery
rubrics_metrics.description: He takes advantage of all the most trite and mechanical common-places of imagery and diction ... fills up the intervals of true inspiration with the most vapid and worthless materials.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Originality in image-making is essential; do not fill gaps in inspiration with stock phrases or tired conceits.

rubrics_metrics.name: Balance spontaneous feeling with craft and revision
rubrics_metrics.description: His art is as naked and undisguised as his nature ... he takes no pains, uses no self-correction; or if he seems to labour, it is worse than labour lost.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Spontaneity and natural feeling are virtues, but they should be tempered with craft, revision and technical care; leaving everything to chance risks uneven quality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consideration of audience taste vs fidelity in translation/adaptation
rubrics_metrics.description: His alterations from Chaucer and Boccaccio shew a greater knowledge of the taste of his readers and power of pleasing them, than acquaintance with the genius of his authors. He ekes out the lameness of the verse and breaks the force of the passion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Translators/adapters must balance pleasing contemporary readers with preserving the original's force and genius; pandering to taste can weaken the source's power.

rubrics_metrics.name: Heroical magnanimity in satirical epithets
rubrics_metrics.description: There is a magnanimity of abuse in some of these epithets, a fearless choice of topics of invective, which may be considered as the heroical in satire.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Boldness and moral grandeur in satire (fearless choice of topics) can elevate invective beyond mere malice into principled critique.

rubrics_metrics.name: Diction: avoid bombastic allusion or overloading fine lines
rubrics_metrics.description: He overloads an exquisitely natural sentiment or image with a cloud of painted, pompous, cumbrous phrases, like the shower of roses ...
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not spoil fine moments with turgid allusion or inflated language; aim for fitting diction and clarity that supports, not overwhelms, the impression.

rubrics_metrics.name: Dramatic writing should transcend rhetorical commonplaces
rubrics_metrics.description: Dryden's plays ... though he does not go out of himself by the force of imagination, he goes out of himself by the force of common-places and rhetorical dialogue.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Good drama requires imaginative transcendence beyond rhetorical or commonplace declamation; characters and situations should feel lived-in, not merely rhetorical vehicles.
